request.prompt:
An elevation of the whole abandoned saltworks at Greyhithe seen from the open water to the west, the eye a little above the waves, the whole site in one frame from left to right.

Left, at the waterline: a shingle beach under a low cliff, a wrecked timber jetty. Beyond it, half-drowned in the sea, six rectangular evaporating pans with their stone walls broken and the water standing in them.

Centre, one storey up on a cut terrace: the works. The great boiling house is the largest building, a long stone hall about thirty-two paces square and fourteen high, four square chimneys along its ridge, a row of tall narrow round-headed clerestory windows the whole length of it. Beside it a walled coal yard open to the sky, a narrow hoist tower, a low store with the same high windows, and an open yard.

Right, one storey higher again: the abbey precinct behind a wall, its church the tallest building on the site, the same height and the same window rhythm as the boiling house so that the two read as one hand.

Far right, at the end of a bare headland that falls to the sea on both sides: a squat stone light tower, and a single warm lamp burning at the top of it.

The whole thing reads as one silhouette against the dusk: low at the water, rising in two steps, and ending in the light.
request.style_note: The Saltworks at Greyhithe, in one hand throughout: a cold North Sea dusk, the sky a narrow band of pale light low in the west and dark above. One masonry everywhere — grey lias limestone laid in long thin courses, iron-stained red-brown where the sea reaches it, quoins and jambs in the same stone dressed square. One way of letting light in — tall narrow round-headed openings in a repeated rhythm, high in the wall, in the works and in the abbey alike. Slate roofs weathered near-black, salt-bleached timber, no render, no whitewash. One warm lamp burning on the headland, the only warm colour in the picture. Matte gouache on toned grey paper, restrained palette, visible dry brush, no figures, no text, no lettering. Each image is ONE single full-frame view of that place, filling the frame edge to edge: never a sheet, never a grid, never a panel, never an inset or a caption.
